title: Idiomatic C# after five years
hook: Five years of shipping .NET is visible in names, in what you make public, and in what you refuse to clever. It is not visible in using every C# 14 syntax toy.

sections.heading: Names the platform already agreed on
sections.prose: The compiler accepts many identifiers; .NET convention does not. PascalCase for types, namespaces, and public members. Interfaces start with `I`. Attribute types end with `Attribute`. Enums: singular unless they are flags. camelCase for parameters and locals. Private/internal instance fields: `_camelCase`. Static fields: `s_`, thread-static: `t_` (runtime style; not the Visual Studio default). Constants: PascalCase even when private. No consecutive `__` — the compiler reserves those. Type parameters: `T` or `TSession`. Primary constructor parameters: camelCase on classes/structs, PascalCase on records because they become properties. Verbatim `@if` is for interop names, not cute locals. Enforce with IDE code-style rules, not a wiki.

snippets.label: A worker type that looks like BCL
snippets.explanation: I-prefix, Async suffix, CancellationToken last, _mux, s_defaultTtl. Interviewers read this in one glance and move on — that is the point of convention.

sections.heading: Language features as defaults, not decorations
sections.prose: Idiomatic 2026 C# uses file-scoped namespaces, NRT enabled (module 07), `using` declarations (module 06), `await` with `ConfigureAwait` only when you are a library that must not capture a sync context (module 13), collection expressions when the target type is obvious (module 08), pattern matching instead of `is` plus cast (module 11), and `Span` on parse hot paths (module 17). It does not use `dynamic`, does not `lock (this)`, does not catch `Exception` to return null, and does not expose `public` fields. Extension members (C# 14) belong in a carefully named static class for a library; they do not belong as a way to hide a God helper. `field` accessors are idiomatic when the extra backing field was noise; they are not idiomatic when you already have a well-named `_email`.

sections.heading: What seniority sounds like
sections.prose: You name the runtime when it matters (module 14 GC, module 15 `Lock`). You keep unsafe in an interop project (module 17). You refuse to make a type public so a test compiles (module 16). You write the SQS handler as a typed method, not reflection. That list is this entire track. Idiomatic C# is the intersection of identifier-names guidance and those engineering defaults — not a second copy of the feature map.

interviewTakeaways: Follow .NET identifier conventions; the compiler will not do it for you.
Prefer the modern defaults (NRT, file-scoped namespaces, patterns, spans) over demonstrating every new keyword.
Senior code hides power (unsafe, reflection, public surface) behind small, named boundaries.
commonPitfalls: Hungarian notation or Java `getFoo` on public C# properties.
Primary constructor parameters on a record named like locals (`firstName`) so the public property looks wrong.
Enabling every C# 14 syntax in a file that still uses `ArrayList`.

jsTsCorrelations.note: JS/TS public fields are typically camelCase. C# public members are PascalCase. Do not “make it look like Node” in a C# library consumed by other C#.
